metaDescription: Five four-color 3D printers compared by color-change cost, expansion path and workflow, so you know what a four-spool setup does and what it wastes.
expertTake: The ELEGOO Centauri 2 Combo is the best four-color pick because the four-spool system comes bundled on a fast CoreXY frame with a beginner-friendly workflow. The FLASHFORGE AD5X is the value pick for small, simple color jobs. Anyone who needs more than four colors per print should look at an expandable system or a toolchanger instead.
introParagraphs: Four colors is the sweet spot for hobby multicolor printing. It covers a character with skin, hair, clothes and an accent, a logo with a background, or a sign with two text colors and a border, without the clutter of a sixteen-spool rack.

How a machine swaps those four colors decides what you pay in time and plastic. This guide ranks five four-color printers on their color-change method, their expansion path and the real workflow of designing, slicing and finishing a multicolor print.

products.name: ELEGOO Centauri 2 Combo with CANVAS four-color system, 500 mm/s CoreXY
products.description:
The Centauri 2 Combo bundles the CANVAS system, which holds four spools and feeds one nozzle, with a 500 mm/s CoreXY machine. Because the feeder is part of the package, setup is shorter than adding a feeder to a standalone printer. The maker pitches it at beginners, and the combined workflow is the main appeal.

A single-nozzle four-color machine swaps colors by retracting one filament and loading the next, then purging the nozzle clean. That swap takes time and plastic on every change, so a model with hundreds of changes prints slowly and wastes filament. Against the FLASHFORGE AD5X, it offers a faster headline speed and a newer platform. Against the Creator 5, it costs far less and wastes more.

Ownership centers on dry spools and clear filament paths. Check parts availability since the platform is newer, keep firmware updates deliberate, and buy filament with consistent diameter so the feeder does not jam.
products.bestFor: Newcomers who want a bundled, fast four-color workflow.
pros: Four-spool CANVAS bundled with the printer
Enclosed-style platform from an established maker
cons: Purge waste on every color change
Newer platform with a shorter parts history
Four colors is the ceiling in this bundle

products.name: ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 Combo with CANVAS, multicolor 500 mm/s printer
products.description:
The Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a sibling listing in the same line, also with the CANVAS four-color system, 500 mm/s CoreXY motion and one-click automatic leveling. The Carbon branding points to a version aimed at stiffer, higher-temperature materials. The listing details overlap heavily with the Centauri 2 Combo, so compare the exact specifications on the page.

The workflow is the same: four spools, one nozzle, purge on every swap, with the same advice to slice for few changes and keep spools dry. Against the Centauri 2 Combo, the choice comes down to which listing offers the better price or feature set at purchase time. Against the AD5X, it is a faster, newer machine.

Ownership matches its sibling. Keep spools dry, clean the filament paths, and note that the maker's ecosystem is younger than the market leaders. Confirm warranty terms and spare parts before buying, and read the exact listing carefully, since similar names often hide differences in the feeder, nozzle or included accessories.

pros: Close sibling to the top pick

products.name: FLASHFORGE AD5X four-color printer with IFS and 300 C direct drive
products.description:
The AD5X uses the Intelligent Filament System to feed four spools into one direct-drive nozzle rated to 300 degrees Celsius. The 220 mm cube bed suits figurines, signs and small models, which are the typical four-color jobs. One-click leveling handles bed setup.

It is the lowest-cost route to four colors here, which is the case for it. The tradeoff is the compact build volume and the same purge waste as any single-nozzle system. Against the Centauri 2 Combo, it offers a higher headline speed and a hotter nozzle but a different software workflow.

Ownership is routine: dry spools, clean paths, spare nozzles and the usual belt and rail care. The tool-free nozzle swap on the platform makes clogs a minor event, and the printer is widely stocked.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want four colors at the lowest tier.

products.name: ANYCUBIC Kobra X Fast native four-color printer with ACE 2 Pro, up to 19 colors
products.description:
The Kobra X starts with native four-color printing and expands to a listed maximum of 19 colors with extra ACE 2 Pro units. That expansion path is the reason to choose it: you can start at four and grow without changing printers. It arrives pre-assembled with a modular design and automatic leveling.

Expansion has a price, since each unit adds cost, desk space and spools to dry. Against the AD5X, it offers a growth path but no hotter nozzle. Against the Creator 5, it keeps the single-nozzle system, so waste remains high.

Ownership is about keeping more spools in good condition. Store them dry, label slots clearly and watch tube paths as you add units. Many buyers never go past four, so decide whether you need the room before paying for it.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want to start at four colors and grow.
pros: Native four colors with expansion to 19
cons: Expansion units add cost and bench space
Same purge waste on every swap
More spools to dry as you grow

products.name: FLASHFORGE Creator 5 four-toolhead changer, near-zero waste multicolor
products.description:
The Creator 5 uses four independent toolheads that swap onto the carriage, so each color has its own nozzle and no purge is needed between changes. The listing calls it a near-zero waste system. It also handles true multi-material jobs, such as rigid plus flexible filament.

The cost is price and complexity, since four hotends mean four sets of parts to maintain and calibrate. Against the single-nozzle machines, it removes purge waste entirely, which can pay back on color-heavy production. Against the AD5X, it is a very different tier.

Ownership means calibrating nozzle offsets, keeping spares and handling a more complex machine. It suits workshops and small sellers, not casual owners. For a seller printing fifty identical multicolor keychains, the saved plastic and shorter job time add up quickly, while for a hobbyist printing one figure a month the savings never cover the extra cost of the machine.
products.bestFor: Color-heavy production where purge waste is the main cost.
cons: Four hotends to calibrate and maintain

buyingCriteria.explanation: A single-nozzle four-color machine swaps filament through one nozzle and purges between colors. A toolchanger such as the Creator 5 swaps entire nozzles and wastes almost nothing. The first costs less and wastes plastic, the second costs more and saves it. Choose by how many color changes your typical model has, and be honest about it: a buyer who prints one color most days and a color figure monthly is better served by a cheaper machine and a bit of paint.

Each change takes time to retract, load, prime and purge. A model with hundreds of changes can print for hours longer and waste more plastic than the object weighs. Count color changes in the slicer before you print a model, which takes seconds, and design objects with large single-color regions. A rule of thumb many owners use is to look at the estimated filament total: if the purge and tower weight exceeds the part itself, redesign the model or paint the small details by hand. Layer-by-layer color changes, such as a gradient or text on every layer, are the worst case, while a single color change at one height is almost free.

The Kobra X expands from four to a listed 19 colors with extra units. The Centauri and AD5X bundles are fixed at four. If you expect to need more colors, an expandable system saves a second purchase; if not, it is an expense you never use. Remember too that slicer limits and tower size can cap how many colors a single model can sensibly use, whatever the hardware allows.

A bundled system tends to have profiles and presets that make color assignment easy. The Centauri 2 Combo is pitched at beginners. Evaluate how the slicer handles painting regions and purge towers, because that workflow is where you spend your time. Look for a slicer that previews each color region, estimates waste and lets you shrink the tower or print the purge inside infill. The best hardware is frustrating if assigning a color takes ten clicks per region, and the worst slicer hides waste until the print is already running.

The AD5X offers a 220 mm cube, enough for figurines and signs. Large multicolor props need bigger beds. Match the bed to your typical project, not your best-case dream. Four-color jobs are often small, so a compact bed is rarely the limit, but remember that the purge tower takes space on the plate, which reduces the usable area by a noticeable margin on a small bed.

Four spools sit in open air unless the system dries them, and moist filament strings and jams. Plan for sealed storage or a dryer, and use spools that unwind freely. Spools in a feeder sit for days, so a model that waits a week between color jobs deserves a fresh drying cycle, and mixing a damp spool with three dry ones will spoil the whole print.

howWeEvaluated.title: Color-change method
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared single-nozzle feeders and the toolchanger on waste and time per swap. The Creator 5 scored best on waste.

howWeEvaluated.title: Expansion
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how far each system can grow. The Kobra X leads.

howWeEvaluated.title: Workflow
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed bundling, presets and slicer support. Bundled combos scored higher because they ship with tuned profiles and a ready workflow, which matters more to a new color printer than raw speed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at speed, nozzle limits and build volume, treating headline speed as a ceiling and giving more weight to nozzle temperature and bed size.

howWeEvaluated.title: Upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted dry-storage and maintenance chores, and favored systems that are easy to service and whose parts are sold directly.

rows: May need more than four colors

cards.label: Feeder
cards.text: The Centauri, AD5X and Kobra X swap spools through one nozzle. They cost less and waste plastic on every change.

cards.label: Toolchanger
cards.text: The Creator 5 swaps nozzles. It wastes almost nothing but costs more and has more parts.

howToChoose.note: Choose a feeder for hobby color. Choose a toolchanger when waste is a business cost, such as when you sell dozens of identical multicolor items and every gram of filament counts toward profit.

howToChoose.subheading: For Multicolor Signs and Logos Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Large flat color regions, few swaps and a clean purge tower. Signs are ideal for four-color systems because the colors sit in layers: a base color, a raised text color and a border, so only a handful of swaps are needed across the whole print.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The AD5X suits small signs, and the Creator 5 suits runs of identical signs where waste adds up.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You print many color parts or sell them. The Creator 5 pays back in saved plastic.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You print a few color models a month. The AD5X or Centauri covers it.

maintenance.why: Feeders leave spools exposed. Moist filament strings and snaps, which is especially painful mid-way through a long color print.
Shavings cause jams, and a soft brush or compressed air clears them in seconds.
Only on the toolchanger. Misaligned heads blur color edges, so print a small test pattern after any nozzle swap and adjust the offsets until the lines meet cleanly.
Fast machines stretch belts and dry rails, and the extra swaps in a color job mean more motion per print, so keep to the schedule.
Frequent swaps and flow wear tips, and a worn nozzle shows up first as softer detail at color boundaries.

faq.a: For most figurines, signs and logos, yes. More colors help with detailed art but multiply waste and storage, and many striking prints use just two or three colors with clever design, so try mastering four before paying for expansion.

faq.q: How much plastic does a color change waste?
faq.a: It varies by slicer settings and model. Many changes can waste more than the part uses, and the slicer's filament estimate usually shows the purge total before you start, so check it first and redesign if it looks excessive.

faq.q: Can I print one color on these machines?
faq.a: Yes. They print single-color jobs like any printer, using one slot, so the color system never gets in the way of ordinary functional parts.
Only if waste or multi-material parts matter to you, which usually means production or engineering use rather than casual hobby printing.

faq.q: Do I need to paint models instead?
faq.a: Painting avoids purge waste and gives fine detail, but takes time and skill. Many owners combine both, printing the large color regions and painting eyes, text and small accents by hand.
It can with wet or tangled filament. Dry spools and clear paths prevent most jams, and a quick check of each spool's winding before a long job saves a lot of heartbreak.
